# 💼 The case

A transportation agency keeps three years of New York taxi trips as Parquet files in S3, one file
per month. Every quarter it has to report two things: which pickup zones earn their curb space, and
whether a small model can predict fares well enough to argue with. Producing that report takes three
steps, in this order:

1. **Filter and trim the trip files.** Keep only the months in the study window and the valid trips,
   and only the columns the model needs. Most of every file is thrown away.
2. **Build one row per pickup zone.** Join the trips to the zone lookup, then group by zone.
3. **Try a grid of model settings and score each one.** Each setting is checked on 5 folds, held-out
   slices of the data, and every fit is independent of the others.

You will run these steps on a single EC2 instance with DuckDB, then on a Spark cluster on EMR at two
sizes, and compare what each cost. At each step you will be given hints about the size
of the data, which you need to verify against the data itself. We will ask you to estimate the
resources and time each step needs, and to compare your estimates with the real numbers you get as
you go.

DuckDB is a query engine that runs inside a single process and reads Parquet straight out of S3. You
launched the kind of EC2 instance it runs on in A1, and the engine is the new part. Amazon EMR gives
you a Spark cluster you can see, size, and resize.

Your numbers will not be the lecture's numbers, and two of you running the same stage an hour apart
will not agree to the second. Track your own number, compare orders of magnitude, and say why yours
landed where it did.

# Roadmap

```
  39 monthly trip files, Parquet in S3, 19 columns
     |   STAGE 1  DuckDB on one EC2 instance (m7g.xlarge). Scan, filter, project.
     v
  matrix.parquet in S3   +   zones.parquet (265 rows)
     |   STAGE 2a  Spark on EMR at 2 core nodes.
     |   STAGE 2b  the same cluster, resized to 4.
     |            phase A: join and group by pickup zone. phase B: 60 model fits.
     v
  zone features in S3
```

On every stage, we ask you to predict, measure and explain what happens. **Predict** what will happen: give an estimate of performance or price before executing anything. **Measure** what actually happened: run
the stage, and turn the metrics it prints into a row of `results.csv` with
`stages/parse_run_log.py`. **Explain** the difference between your estimate and the measurement, and
name the mechanism behind it, in the notebook, in 2 to 4 sentences.

In predictions we ask for order-of-magnitude comparisons and don't ask for a precise estimate. As a
rule of thumb, you should be able to do a back-of-the-envelope prediction looking at the numbers or
their estimates, seldom needing code or GenAI. Write your prediction down before you launch the run,
then compare it with the measurement. Learning to do these comparisons is how you build data
engineering intuition. You don't get downgraded for wrong predictions.

::: {.callout-note icon=false title="🗺️ Shape of the work"}
Work in stage order: every Spark run reads `matrix.parquet`, which Stage 1 writes. Setup comes first: the
roles, the bucket, and the data fetch, which runs for a few minutes on its own while you read ahead.
Stage 1 then writes `matrix.parquet`, and nothing in Stages 2a or 2b can run until that file
exists.

Stages 2a and 2b run on one cluster, which you launch at 2 core nodes and then resize in place to
4. Two waits there are normal, and neither means anything is wrong: the
cluster takes minutes to reach `WAITING` after the create call, and after a resize the new nodes
report as running some way before Spark has an executor on each of them.

Question 4 needs no cloud at all. You answer it from `results.csv` and your own run logs, so it is the part
to leave until after everything is terminated. What you hand in is the notebook with every
prediction written before its run, `results.csv` with its 5 rows, and 2 screenshots.
:::

## Your shells and variables {#variables}

Everything in this assignment runs in the AWS console, in your browser. There is no AWS command to
run on your laptop, which only keeps `results.csv` and your screenshots. Two shells do the work:

- **CloudShell**, a terminal inside the AWS console (the `>_` icon in the top bar). It already has
  the AWS CLI and your credentials, and it runs every command except the Stage 1 job itself.
- **Session Manager** on the Stage 1 instance, which you open from the EC2 console. It runs the
  Stage 1 job.

| Commands | Shell | What has to stay running |
|---|---|---|
| [Once per account](#once-per-account), [Get the data](#get-the-data) | CloudShell | the tab, until the fetch loop finishes. CloudShell's home directory survives closing it |
| `run-instances` in [Stage 1 on one EC2 instance](#stage-1-on-one-ec2-instance) | CloudShell | nothing |
| the Stage 1 run itself, and its parse | Session Manager on the Stage 1 instance | the tab, for the length of the run. Anything written to that disk dies when you terminate the instance |
| creating the cluster in [Launch the cluster](#launch-the-cluster) | the EMR console, in your browser | nothing. Its **AWS CLI export** goes into `launch-cluster.sh` in CloudShell |
| the rest of [Launch the cluster](#launch-the-cluster) through [Resize and re-run](#resize-and-re-run), and [Shut down and verify](#shut-down-and-verify) | CloudShell | nothing in the shell. The cluster runs on AWS whether the tab is open or not |
| `results.csv` and the two screenshots | your laptop | they stay on your laptop from the first row you write to the moment you submit |

The commands name your resources through shell variables such as `$BUCKET`, so you can paste them
unchanged. You set the variables once, in CloudShell. They live in `~/a2.env`, a file in
CloudShell's home folder that survives closing the tab, and a line in `~/.bashrc` loads it into
every new CloudShell tab. In CloudShell, put your CWL in place of `yourcwl`, in lowercase, and run:

```bash
cat > ~/a2.env <<'EOF'
export CWL=yourcwl
export BUCKET=436c-a2-$CWL
save() { export "$1=$2"; echo "export $1=$2" >> ~/a2.env; echo "$1=$2"; }
EOF
grep -qs a2.env ~/.bashrc || echo 'source ~/a2.env' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/a2.env
echo $BUCKET
```

The last line prints `436c-a2-` and your CWL. Every other variable is an id AWS hands you along the
way: the subnet, the instance, the cluster, each step. The command that creates each
id saves it with `save`, which adds a line to `~/a2.env`, so you do not type ids by hand. The one
exception is the cluster id, which you copy from the EMR console. `cat ~/a2.env` shows everything
saved so far.

CloudShell also needs `uv`, the Python tool the data step uses, once:

```bash
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
```

## Roles

Three things happen once per account, before anything else: EMR gets the service roles it will not
launch without, your bucket gets created, and the Stage 1 instance gets a role of its own. They are
one block of commands, and it is the first block you run (see 📋 below). A1's role does not
carry over, because it is scoped to the a1 bucket.

[]{#once-per-account}

::::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false title="📋 Commands: Once per account"}
All of this runs in CloudShell. EMR will not launch without its service roles.

```bash
aws emr create-default-roles --region ca-central-1
```

A reply saying the roles already exist is a success. Then make the bucket, in the same region.

```bash
aws s3 mb s3://$BUCKET --region ca-central-1
```

Course accounts have no default network (VPC), so every launch names a subnet. Find the
account's public subnet and save it.

```bash
SUBNET=$(aws ec2 describe-subnets --region ca-central-1 \
  --filters Name=map-public-ip-on-launch,Values=true \
  --query 'Subnets[0].SubnetId' --output text)
save SUBNET "$SUBNET"
```

It prints `SUBNET=subnet-...`, and every launch in this assignment uses that subnet. If it prints
`SUBNET=None`, post on Piazza with your account id and the exact output. Meanwhile you can do
everything up to the launch step: the data fetch and the predictions need no instance.

A2's Stage 1 instance needs its own role, and A1's will not do: A1's is scoped to the a1 bucket and
carries no Session Manager permission. Build the new one the way A1 built its role, create first and
permissions after, then wrap it in an instance profile, which is the object EC2 actually accepts.

```bash
cat > ~/a2-s3-policy.json <<EOF
{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":["s3:GetObject","s3:PutObject","s3:DeleteObject","s3:ListBucket"],"Resource":["arn:aws:s3:::$BUCKET","arn:aws:s3:::$BUCKET/*"]}]}
EOF
aws iam create-role --role-name $CWL-a2-role \
  --assume-role-policy-document '{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"Service":"ec2.amazonaws.com"},"Action":"sts:AssumeRole"}]}'
aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name $CWL-a2-role \
  --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore
aws iam put-role-policy --role-name $CWL-a2-role --policy-name a2-s3 \
  --policy-document file://$HOME/a2-s3-policy.json
aws iam create-instance-profile --instance-profile-name $CWL-a2-role
aws iam add-role-to-instance-profile --instance-profile-name $CWL-a2-role --role-name $CWL-a2-role
```

`AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore` is what lets you open a shell on the instance with no key pair and no
inbound rule. The inline policy is your bucket, and only your bucket. IAM takes about ten seconds to
propagate, so a `run-instances` fired immediately after the last line can come back saying the
instance profile does not exist. Wait, then run it again.

`CWL-a2-role` is the name to put in `INSTANCE_PROFILE` everywhere below.
:::::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="💡 Why a role and not a login"}
A general (simplified!) rule: instances and services get roles, people get accounts with logins. If you need to
assign some permissions to an EC2 instance or an EMR cluster, you need to create a role
allowing them to do something on your behalf. Remember that in A1 we created instance and execution
roles; here in A2 we use the default EMR service roles and create one role for the Stage 1 instance
following the 📋 commands below. Every time you see an "access denied" type of
error, you need to check for a missing role, or a permission you need to add.
:::

## Bucket and data {#bucket-and-data}

Create `s3://436c-a2-<your CWL>/` and put 40 objects in it: the 39 monthly trip files from the New
York Taxi and Limousine Commission (TLC) distribution, and the zone lookup, which arrives as CSV
and is converted to Parquet once as `zones.parquet`. The
fetch loop runs for a few minutes, so start it before you read the rest of this (see 📋 below). The
files travel from the TLC's public file service into your bucket, so nothing here is downloaded to
your laptop.

[]{#get-the-data}

::::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false title="📋 Commands: Get the data"}
Thirty-nine monthly yellow-taxi files, January 2022 to March 2025, and the zone lookup, straight
from the New York Taxi and Limousine Commission (TLC) distribution into your bucket. Run this in
CloudShell, before the Stage 1 instance exists. It moves about 2 GB and takes a few minutes, so start it before you read ahead. Each file
is deleted after it lands in S3, which keeps the local disk from filling.

```bash
for Y in 2022 2023 2024; do
  for M in 01 02 03 04 05 06 07 08 09 10 11 12; do
    curl -sSfO "https://d37ci6vzurychx.cloudfront.net/trip-data/yellow_tripdata_${Y}-${M}.parquet"
    aws s3 cp "yellow_tripdata_${Y}-${M}.parquet" s3://$BUCKET/a2/raw/ --region ca-central-1
    rm "yellow_tripdata_${Y}-${M}.parquet"
  done
done

for M in 2025-01 2025-02 2025-03; do
  curl -sSfO "https://d37ci6vzurychx.cloudfront.net/trip-data/yellow_tripdata_${M}.parquet"
  aws s3 cp "yellow_tripdata_${M}.parquet" s3://$BUCKET/a2/raw/ --region ca-central-1
  rm "yellow_tripdata_${M}.parquet"
done
```

The lookup ships as CSV. The Stage 2a job reads it as Parquet, with the columns `LocationID`,
`Borough`, and `Zone`, so convert it once before you need it.

```bash
curl -sSfO "https://d37ci6vzurychx.cloudfront.net/misc/taxi_zone_lookup.csv"
uv run --with duckdb python3 -c "
import duckdb
duckdb.sql('''COPY (SELECT LocationID, Borough, Zone
                    FROM read_csv_auto('taxi_zone_lookup.csv'))
              TO 'zones.parquet' (FORMAT PARQUET)''')
"
aws s3 cp zones.parquet s3://$BUCKET/a2/raw/zones.parquet --region ca-central-1
```

Check what landed before you launch anything. You want 40 objects: 39 trip files and
`zones.parquet`. A short count means a `curl` failed partway through the loop, so re-run it: the
files already in the bucket are simply overwritten.

```bash
aws s3 ls s3://$BUCKET/a2/raw/ --summarize --human-readable --region ca-central-1
```

Prediction 1 starts from the size of the trip files, so total those 39 on their own. The lookup is
not part of what Stage 1 reads.

```bash
aws s3 ls s3://$BUCKET/a2/raw/yellow_tripdata_ --summarize --human-readable --region ca-central-1
```
:::::

## The results file

`results.csv` ships with the assignment, header only. Keep it on your laptop, from the first row you
write to the moment you submit, and append one row per stage-phase there: five rows in all, one for
Stage 1 and two each for Stages 2a and 2b. Nothing you run in the cloud writes to this file. The
Stage 1 instance is terminated before you hand anything in, so a copy that lives only on it is a
copy you lose.

Four of its columns need explaining. `resource_id` is the instance or cluster ID, and
it has to match a screenshot. `predicted_s` is your prediction, entered **before** the run.
`wall_s` and `startup_s` stay in separate columns. `cost_usd` comes from AWS's price pages for [EC2 on-demand instances](https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/pricing/on-demand/)
and [EMR](https://aws.amazon.com/emr/pricing/), read for ca-central-1, not from the billing console.

The order of work within a row is fixed. Write that row's `predicted_s` from the prediction block
first, before you launch anything. Then run the stage, tee its
output to a log file, and hand the log to [`stages/parse_run_log.py`](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/a2-starter/blob/main/stages/parse_run_log.py), which prints the measured row to
the shell with `predicted_s` empty by design. Copy the measured values into the row you already
wrote, or paste the printed row in and type your prediction back into it. The parser never produces
`predicted_s`. That number is yours, and the notebook cell you wrote it in is what dates it.

Before you parse a log, glance at [Did the run work?](#did-the-run-work) below:
four lines that tell you whether the run is worth reading at all.

[]{#did-the-run-work}

::::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false title="📋 Did the run work?"}
Four lines to glance at in a log before you parse it. If any of them is wrong, the run is not
comparable to your others, and re-running is the only fix.

- **The block arrived.** `grep -c '===A2-METRICS' YOUR.log` prints 1 for Stage 1 and 2 for Stages 2a
  and 2b. A 0 means the script stopped early, and the reason sits above where the block should
  have been.
The first check applies to every run. The other three apply to the Spark runs only: Stage 1's
block reads `mode=duckdb` and has no retry or shuffle keys.

- **`mode=rest`** in every Stage 2 block, with `rest_target` naming the host the metrics reader reached. A
  cluster run that exits 3 reached no Spark REST endpoint and measured nothing. That is a
  failed run, not a slow one.
- **`retried=0`.** A 1 means a stage or task was retried, so the timings are not comparable: rerun.
- **`shuffle_partitions` reads 16**, and `partitions` in the phase A block reads the same 16. If the
  two disagree, the shuffle setting did not take and your two node counts stop being comparable.
  The one run where both read 8 instead is the optional extension below, and it is the only one.
  `tasks` is a different number and is meant to move with the cluster.
:::::

# Stage 1. DuckDB on one EC2 instance {#stage-1}

⚙️ **Data engineering:** what one instance costs in time to read a large Parquet dataset out of
S3, and how much of each file it has to move to do it.

[`stages/stage1_duckdb.py`](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/a2-starter/blob/main/stages/stage1_duckdb.py) points DuckDB at the raw trip files in S3. It filters to the study window,
January 2022 through March 2025, and to valid records, keeps the 6 columns the model needs out of
the 19 each file carries (20 in the 2025 files), and writes the result back to S3 as
`matrix.parquet`, the model matrix Stage 2a reads. It runs on one EC2
instance, an `m7g.xlarge` with 4 vCPU, with no cluster involved, and measures one pass over data: read rows, drop most of them, write what is
left. 

Before that pass it reads the same columns once without writing, so that `t_read_s` prices
the read on its own. The supplied stage runs in one DuckDB process. The stages after it use Spark on an EMR cluster for the join, the grouping and the model fits.

## 1.1 Predict

`rubric={reasoning:5}`

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="📐 Prediction 1, how long will Stage 1 take?"}
```
predicted_seconds ≈ bytes_to_read / read_rate
```

- **Bytes to read.** In CloudShell, total the size of the 39 trip files:

  ```bash
  aws s3 ls s3://$BUCKET/a2/raw/yellow_tripdata_ --summarize --human-readable --region ca-central-1
  ```

  The script reads 6 of the 19 columns in each file. The 2025 files have one extra column, which
  you don't need. Based on this, estimate how much data you expect to read. Give a
  one- or two-sentence explanation.
- **Read rate.** The instance page lists the `m7g.xlarge` network as "up to 12.5 Gb/s". Write the
  rate you will actually use in your prediction, in bytes per second, and where it came from.

All data has to come through the network before DuckDB can read it, so the network is one
candidate limit (L2's throughput table). Compare the rate you achieve with it, and say what else
could be the limit (L4: the CPU that decompresses and parses).

Write your prediction into the `predicted_s` cell of your Stage 1 row before you run the stage. The
script prints the measured time, so run it only after your prediction is written.
:::

The parser will key that row `stage=1_duckdb`, `phase=scan`.

## 1.2 Measure

`rubric={correctness:5}`

Launch one `m7g.xlarge` with your CWL in the name from CloudShell, then run the script from a
shell on the instance itself (see 📋 below). It prints one metrics block.

[]{#stage-1-on-one-ec2-instance}

::::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false title="📋 Commands: Stage 1 on one EC2 instance"}
From CloudShell, launch one `m7g.xlarge` on Amazon Linux 2023 with the instance profile you made
under [Once per account](#once-per-account).

```bash
INSTANCE_ID=$(aws ec2 run-instances --region ca-central-1 \
  --image-id resolve:ssm:/aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-arm64 \
  --instance-type m7g.xlarge \
  --count 1 \
  --subnet-id $SUBNET \
  --iam-instance-profile Name=$CWL-a2-role \
  --block-device-mappings 'DeviceName=/dev/xvda,Ebs={VolumeSize=60,VolumeType=gp3}' \
  --tag-specifications "ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=a2-stage1-$CWL}]" \
  --query 'Instances[0].InstanceId' --output text)
save INSTANCE_ID "$INSTANCE_ID"
```

The root volume is sized at 60 GiB because the AL2023 default of 8 GiB leaves little room once the
Python toolchain and its packages are installed. The raw files never touch this disk: DuckDB reads
them from S3 and writes its result back there. `/dev/xvda` is AL2023's root device name. The image name ends in `arm64` because
an `m7g.xlarge` is a Graviton (ARM) instance, and an `x86_64` image does not boot on it. If you launch
from the console instead, pick the 64-bit (Arm) architecture for the same reason.

Connect from the EC2 console: select the instance, choose Connect, then the Session Manager tab.
There is no key pair and no inbound SSH rule anywhere in this assignment. The session opens in
`/usr/bin`, a folder you cannot write to, so the first line below moves to your home folder. Then
clone the repo and work from its root, because [`stages/stage1_duckdb.py`](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/a2-starter/blob/main/stages/stage1_duckdb.py) imports a helper out of
[`stages/stage2_spark.py`](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/a2-starter/blob/main/stages/stage2_spark.py) and a single copied file will not run.

In CloudShell, run `cat ~/a2.env` and copy the lines that start with `export`. Paste them into the
Session Manager shell, so `$BUCKET` and `$INSTANCE_ID` mean the same thing there.

```bash
cd ~
sudo dnf install -y git
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
git clone https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/a2-starter.git && cd a2-starter
```

Now run the stage and keep the output.

```bash
uv run --python 3.11 \
  --with duckdb --with pyspark --with numpy --with "pandas<3" --with pyyaml \
  python3 stages/stage1_duckdb.py \
    --trips "s3://$BUCKET/a2/raw/yellow_tripdata_*.parquet" \
    --out s3://$BUCKET/a2/matrix.parquet \
    --window-start 2022-01-01 --window-end 2025-04-01 \
  | tee stage1.log
```

The `--trips` glob is quoted so DuckDB expands the `*`, not your shell. `--python 3.11` overrides
the system Python, which on Amazon Linux 2023 is 3.9. `pyspark`, `numpy`, and `pandas` are there
for one import at the top of the script and run none of the query.

If the run stops on a `Secret Validation Failure` before it prints anything, the instance has no
credentials to sign the S3 reads with: the instance profile is missing from the instance, so attach
`INSTANCE_PROFILE` to the instance and run it again.

Turn the log into a `results.csv` row. Confirm the metrics block arrived first: `grep -c
'===A2-METRICS' stage1.log` prints 1.

```bash
python3 stages/parse_run_log.py stage1.log --resource-id $INSTANCE_ID --nodes 1
```

It prints the row to the shell and writes nothing. Copy what it prints into the `results.csv` on
your laptop, next to the prediction you put in that row before the run: the parser leaves
`predicted_s` empty every time, and your own copy of the file is the only place that number exists.

Once its row is on your laptop and screenshot 1 is taken, nothing later needs the instance:
[Shut down and verify](#shut-down-and-verify) terminates it, and you can do that now.
:::::

| Key | What it is |
|---|---|
| `wall_s` | the run's duration, and what the parser puts in your Stage 1 row |
| `bytes_on_disk` | compressed size of every column in the files it opened |
| `bytes_needed` | compressed size of the 6 columns it read |
| `rows_in`, `rows_out` | rows before the filter, rows after |
| `mb_per_s_per_core` | the per-core read rate the run achieved |

Parse the log into your Stage 1 row and fill in `cost_usd` from the EC2 rate for ca-central-1.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="📸 Screenshot 1"}
The instance page while it runs: instance ID, type, launch time, CWL in the name. The instance ID
must equal `resource_id` in your Stage 1 row.
:::

:::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="👀 Quick check"}
- `bytes_needed` should be well below `bytes_on_disk` but not tiny: the columns are of different
  size. If it comes back at zero, or equal to `bytes_on_disk`, the run did not work: run it again.
- The rate you achieved should land well below the advertised 12.5 Gb/s. If yours lands above it,
  check your units: the metrics key is megabytes per second, the instance page gigabits per second.
- The timed pass, `wall_s`, should take well under a minute.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false title="Compare with our run, open after you have written your explanation"}
In our runs almost all of Stage 1's wall time was the read. The filter and the write cost very
little next to it.
:::
::::

# Stage 2a. The cluster at 2 core nodes

⚙️ **Data engineering:** the same job on two cluster sizes, and what doubling the nodes does to
each of its two phases.

[`stages/stage2_spark.py`](https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/a2-starter/blob/main/stages/stage2_spark.py) reads `matrix.parquet`, which Stage 1 wrote, and runs two phases against
it.

Spark runs a job as one *driver*, the process that plans the work, and some number of *executors*,
the processes that do it, one or more per node in the cluster. It splits the data into
*partitions*, chunks of rows, and hands partitions out to executors. A partition is worked on by one
core.

Phase `A_aggregate` sends a copy of the 265-row zone lookup, `zones.parquet`, to every executor (a
*broadcast*, which is cheap because the lookup is a few hundred rows), joins it to
`matrix.parquet`, then groups by pickup zone. The group-by is a wide dependency: every zone's rows have to meet in one place before
they can be aggregated, so every row first goes into the *shuffle* (an `Exchange` in L6's plans), and
only the rows meant for another node travel over the network. `shuffle_write_bytes` is what the shuffle costs. The job fixes the number of those places at
16 shuffle partitions, the same 16 at either node count, and the
stage after the shuffle has 16 pieces of work to hand out. The job turns off adaptive execution's
merging of small partitions (L6), so the 16 stay 16.

Phase `B_fit` searches the grid: 12 combinations on 5 folds, 60 fits, each independent of the
others. No join, no shuffle, one task per fit.

You run this file twice, at 2 core nodes and then at 4, on EMR release `emr-spark-8.0.0`. A scaling
claim needs two points, so this is the one repeat in the assignment. That release runs Spark 4, and
L6's Spark UI pages come from Spark 3.5, so expect small differences in the UI.

## 2a.1 Predict

`rubric={reasoning:4}`

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="📐 Prediction 2, how long will phase A take?"}
```
time_A ≈ rows / (cores × rows_per_second_per_core)
```

- **Rows.** `rows_out` from your Stage 1 metrics block, which is what `matrix.parquet` holds. Write
  the number down.
- **Rows per second per core.** Stage 1's `rows_out` divided by its `wall_s`, divided again by its
  4 cores. That rate prices a scan and phase A also aggregates, so write the rate you are using and
  say that it makes your answer a floor.
- **Cores.** Core nodes times the 4 vCPU an `m7g.xlarge` has. No task runs on the primary node (L5), so
  count only core-node cores. Write the core count you are predicting with.

Phase A has 16 partitions to hand out and a partition is worked on by one core, so 8 cores work
through them in two waves and 16 cores in one. Say what that does to the formula above at each
node count.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="📐 Prediction 3, how long will phase B take?"}
```
time_B ≈ ceil(fits / cores) × seconds_per_fit
```

- **Fits.** 60, from 12 combinations on 5 folds. The job prints it back as `fits_done`. Write it
  into the formula.
- **Seconds per fit.** You have measured no fit yet, so write a defensible estimate with one
  sentence of reasoning. After the 2-node run you replace it with a measured figure.
- **Cores.** The same core count as in prediction 2.

Phase B has 60 independent fits and no shuffle. Each core runs one fit at a time, so the fits go in
waves of as many fits as you have cores. `ceil` rounds up because a last, partly full wave still
takes a whole fit's time (L6).
:::

Both predictions go into `results.csv` before you submit the step.

## 2a.2 Measure

`rubric={correctness:4}`

::: {.callout-warning icon=false title="⚠️ Finish Setup's bucket and data, and Stage 1, before you start the cluster"}
The cluster writes its logs to `s3://436c-a2-<your CWL>/a2/emr-logs/`, and every step reads
`matrix.parquet`, which [Stage 1](#stage-1) writes to the same bucket. The bucket and its data
come from [Bucket and data](#bucket-and-data) in Setup. Check both before you choose **Create
cluster**: `aws s3 ls s3://436c-a2-<your CWL>/a2/` should list `raw/` and `matrix.parquet`. A
cluster started without them bills from the moment it launches and can do nothing useful, and a
step submitted without `matrix.parquet` fails with *The given path is invalid*.
:::

Build the cluster in the EMR console: 1 primary and 2 core `m7g.xlarge`, release `emr-spark-8.0.0`,
Spark, the idle termination setting left on, and your CWL in the cluster name. Before you leave the
cluster page, export its definition as a CLI command and save it as `launch-cluster.sh`. If the
cluster terminates, that command rebuilds it exactly. The settings, the export, and the fallback
are in the 📋 block below. Every command from here to the end of the assignment runs in
CloudShell.

[]{#launch-the-cluster}

::::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false title="📋 Console steps and commands: Launch the cluster"}
First check that the bucket holds the data and Stage 1's output, because the cluster logs to it and
every step reads from it. The bucket comes from [Once per account](#once-per-account), the data from
[Get the data](#get-the-data), and `matrix.parquet` from [Stage 1 on one EC2 instance](#stage-1-on-one-ec2-instance).

```bash
aws s3 ls s3://$BUCKET/a2/        # expect raw/ and matrix.parquet
```

In the EMR console (**EMR on EC2 → Clusters → Create cluster**), set these and leave everything
else at its default:

- **Name and applications**: cluster name `a2-` followed by your CWL; Amazon EMR release `emr-spark-8.0.0`, picked
  exactly, since the console offers later `8.0.x` releases and those are different builds;
  application bundle **Spark**
- **Cluster configuration**: instance groups, with **Primary** 1 × `m7g.xlarge` and **Core**
  2 × `m7g.xlarge`; remove the Task group if the wizard offers one
- **Networking**: your subnet, which `echo $SUBNET` prints in CloudShell
- **Cluster termination**: keep automatic termination after idle time on, and set it to
  **15 minutes**. It is the difference between a $2 assignment and a $60 one if you close your
  laptop at the wrong moment
- **Cluster logs**: the path `echo s3://$BUCKET/a2/emr-logs/` prints in CloudShell
- **IAM roles**: service role `EMR_DefaultRole`, instance profile `EMR_EC2_DefaultRole`, the two
  that `create-default-roles` made

Choose **Create cluster**. On the cluster's page, choose **AWS CLI export** and paste the command
it shows into a new file in CloudShell, `launch-cluster.sh`.
It reads like this, with your own subnet and bucket where this shows `$SUBNET` and `$BUCKET`:

```bash
aws emr create-cluster --region ca-central-1 \
  --name "a2-$CWL" \
  --release-label emr-spark-8.0.0 \
  --applications Name=Spark \
  --ec2-attributes SubnetId=$SUBNET \
  --instance-groups \
      InstanceGroupType=MASTER,InstanceCount=1,InstanceType=m7g.xlarge \
      InstanceGroupType=CORE,InstanceCount=2,InstanceType=m7g.xlarge \
  --use-default-roles \
  --auto-termination-policy IdleTimeout=900 \
  --log-uri s3://$BUCKET/a2/emr-logs/
```

Check three things in the copy: the release label, `InstanceCount=2` on the CORE group, and
`IdleTimeout=900`. If the cluster terminates before you are done, run `bash launch-cluster.sh` in
CloudShell or repeat the console steps. Either builds the same cluster again.

The cluster id, `j-...`, is on the cluster page. It is the one id you copy by hand: put yours in
place of the `j-` value below.

```bash
save CLUSTER_ID j-XXXXXXXXXXXXX
```

Then poll until the state reads `WAITING`. The same call returns the launch's start and end, so you do not time it
yourself.

```bash
aws emr describe-cluster --cluster-id $CLUSTER_ID --region ca-central-1 \
  --query 'Cluster.Status.{State:State,Created:Timeline.CreationDateTime,Ready:Timeline.ReadyDateTime}'
```

`launch_s` is `Ready` minus `Created`, in seconds. The EMR console shows the same two stamps under
the cluster's timeline if you would rather read them there. Save it, with your number in place of
`412`:

```bash
save LAUNCH_S 412
```
:::::

Time the launch: the gap from the create call to the cluster reaching `WAITING` is `launch_s`, which
prediction 4 needs in 2b.3. You pay that wait once and then run twice. Now submit the job as a step (see 📋 below). It prints one metrics block per phase.

[]{#submit-the-job-as-a-step}

::::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false title="📋 Commands: Submit the job as a step"}
CloudShell needs its own copy of the starter repo: the clone you made in Stage 1 lived on the
instance. Clone it here once, then upload the job script. Both EMR runs read this
same object.

```bash
cd ~
[ -d a2-starter ] || git clone https://github.com/cpsc436c-2026w1/a2-starter.git
cd ~/a2-starter
aws s3 cp stages/stage2_spark.py s3://$BUCKET/a2/stages/stage2_spark.py --region ca-central-1
```

Submit it as a step. `--deploy-mode client` keeps the driver
on the primary node, which is what puts its stdout in the step's own log. The step passes no
partition argument, so the job runs at its own default of 16 shuffle partitions and prints that back
as `shuffle_partitions` in every metrics block. Both graded runs use the default.

```bash
STEP_ID=$(aws emr add-steps --cluster-id $CLUSTER_ID --region ca-central-1 \
  --steps "Type=Spark,Name=a2-stage2-2n,ActionOnFailure=CONTINUE,Args=[--deploy-mode,client,s3://$BUCKET/a2/stages/stage2_spark.py,--trips,s3://$BUCKET/a2/matrix.parquet,--zones,s3://$BUCKET/a2/raw/zones.parquet,--out,s3://$BUCKET/a2/stage2-2n,--platform,emr,--fit-rounds,50]" \
  --query 'StepIds[0]' --output text)
save STEP_ID "$STEP_ID"
```

Watch it, and note when it first reports `COMPLETED`.

```bash
aws emr describe-step --cluster-id $CLUSTER_ID --step-id $STEP_ID --region ca-central-1 \
  --query 'Step.Status.{State:State,Start:Timeline.StartDateTime,End:Timeline.EndDateTime}'
```

The script prints its metrics blocks on stdout, which EMR archives under your `--log-uri` a few
minutes after the step ends. Pull it down and unzip it.

```bash
aws s3 cp s3://$BUCKET/a2/emr-logs/$CLUSTER_ID/steps/$STEP_ID/stdout.gz - --region ca-central-1 \
  | gunzip > stage2-2n.log
grep -c '===A2-METRICS' stage2-2n.log      # 2: one for A_aggregate, one for B_fit
```

If the object is not there yet, wait two minutes and repeat. Then parse both blocks into rows.

```bash
python3 stages/parse_run_log.py stage2-2n.log --resource-id $CLUSTER_ID --nodes 2 \
  --startup-s $LAUNCH_S
```

`$LAUNCH_S` is the figure you saved after the launch. It goes on the 2-node rows only,
because the 4-node run reuses the cluster the launch already bought. Both printed rows go into the
`results.csv` on your laptop, the same way Stage 1's did.
:::::

| Key | Phase | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `wall_s` | both | the phase's own timer, first Spark job to last. A phase holds several Spark jobs and stages |
| `shuffle_write_bytes` | A | bytes written out for the shuffle |
| `partitions` | both | the phase's partition count. In phase A this is the pinned 16 |
| `task_med_s`, `task_max_s` | both | the median task of the phase's slowest Spark stage, and the longest task in any of its stages |
| `fits_done`, `effective_parallelism` | B | fits completed, and `min(cores, fits)` as Spark saw it |

Phase B's fits are deliberately not all the same size, so a spread in its task durations is the
design of the grid rather than a finding. Parse both blocks into rows with `nodes=2`.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="📸 Screenshot 2"}
The cluster page while it runs: cluster ID, node count and types, release label, creation time,
CWL in the name. The cluster ID must equal `resource_id` in your `2_emr` rows.
:::

:::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="👀 Quick check"}
- Both phases should complete, and every metrics block should read `retried=0`, with `partitions`
  in the phase A block reading 16.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false title="Compare with our run, open after you have written your explanation in 2b.2"}
In our runs phase A could not finish before its slowest partition did, so `task_max_s` was a large
share of phase A's own `wall_s`.
:::
::::

The explanation for both node counts comes in 2b.2, once the 4-node run gives you the second point.

Write both new predictions into `results.csv`, then resize the cluster to 4 core nodes and re-run

[]{#resize-and-re-run}

::::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false title="📋 Commands: Resize and re-run"}
Grow the cluster in place rather than launching a second one. Find the CORE group first.

```bash
aws emr describe-cluster --cluster-id $CLUSTER_ID --region ca-central-1 \
  --query "Cluster.InstanceGroups[?InstanceGroupType=='CORE'].{Id:Id,Type:InstanceType,Running:RunningInstanceCount,State:Status.State}"
```

```bash
  --query "Cluster.InstanceGroups[?InstanceGroupType=='CORE'].Id | [0]" --output text)
```

Re-run the same `describe-cluster` call until `Running` reads 4 and the group's state is

running some way before Spark has an executor on each of them, and a step that starts early runs

Then submit the identical step with a new output prefix. `save` replaces the step id with the new one.

```bash
  --query 'StepIds[0]' --output text)
save STEP_ID "$STEP_ID"
```

Watch it with the same `describe-step` call as the 2-node run, which now reads the new step id, until it

```bash
aws s3 cp s3://$BUCKET/a2/emr-logs/$CLUSTER_ID/steps/$STEP_ID/stdout.gz - --region ca-central-1 \
  | gunzip > stage2-4n.log
grep -c '===A2-METRICS' stage2-4n.log      # 2
```

Before you parse it, check that the run had all four nodes. The step's driver log prints one
`Registered executor` line for each executor the run gained. Fewer than four means the run never had the whole cluster: the wait was too short and the 4-node run is not comparable to the
2-node one: submit the step again. That log is `stderr.gz`, beside the `stdout.gz` you just pulled.

```bash
aws s3 cp s3://$BUCKET/a2/emr-logs/$CLUSTER_ID/steps/$STEP_ID/stderr.gz - --region ca-central-1 \
  | gunzip | grep -c 'Registered executor'      # 4
python3 stages/parse_run_log.py stage2-4n.log --resource-id $CLUSTER_ID --nodes 4
```

Both runs carry the same `resource_id`, because both ran on the one cluster.

## 2b.3 Keep the cluster up, or launch it for each run?

`rubric={reasoning:10}`

Suppose the agency runs this job several times a day. It can keep the cluster up all day and submit

you measured, `launch_s`, every time; keeping it up costs every idle hour. L7's studio works this
method on lecture numbers.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false title="📐 Prediction 4, how many runs a day before keeping the cluster up costs less?"}

```
N × (launch + work) × cluster_rate = 24 × cluster_rate
```

- **Launch.** Your measured `launch_s`, the gap from the create call to `WAITING`. Write it in hours.

- **Cluster rate.** For one `m7g.xlarge` node, add the ca-central-1 EC2 on-demand rate and the EMR
  rate, then multiply by 3: the primary node is billed too. Write the rate for all three nodes.

The left side launches a cluster for each of N runs in a day and pays for each launch and each run.
The right side keeps one cluster up for all 24 hours. Put every time in hours, solve for the break-even
N, and show the rearrangement as well as the answer. Then give the smallest whole number of runs a day
for which keeping the cluster up costs less.
:::

# Question 4. Which platform, and how to run it

⚙️ **Data engineering:** the pipeline priced end to end, including what the handoffs between stages
cost and what a daily schedule does to the bill.

`rubric={reasoning:25}`

Three questions, each answered from `results.csv` and your own run logs.

## 4.1 Handoffs through S3

Each handoff here is a Parquet round trip through S3: one step writes its result, and the next step
reads it back. No timer measures that on its own, because each write and each read sits inside a
phase's `wall_s` along with the work.

Answer three things:

1. Name the two places where one step writes its result to S3 and the next step reads it back.
2. If all three steps ran in one Spark session on the cluster, which of those writes and reads would
   disappear, and what would you give up in exchange? Think about rerunning only one step, and running
   steps on different machines.
3. Stage 2b doubled the cluster without touching the code or copying the stored data anywhere. What
   about this storage layout made that possible?

## 4.2 Daily cadence

The agency will run this pipeline once a day, indefinitely, as you measured it: Stage 1 on one
instance, the Spark work on EMR. Do you keep the cluster up or launch it for each run? Estimate one
day's compute cost as Stage 1's `wall_s` at the EC2 rate, plus `launch_s` and both Spark phases at the
2-node cluster rate, and say what this estimate leaves out. Use your N from
prediction 4, and name the one change to the workload that would flip your answer.

At 100× the trip volume, which parts do you expect to become significantly slower, and which to fail

Check first that `results.csv` and your two screenshots are on your laptop. Terminating the


Confirm both state changes on the console list pages.

Then check your budget the next morning, and again the morning after. A command that exits cleanly
proves the API accepted your request. First confirm `TERMINATED` on the EC2 and EMR console pages.
The spend on the next two mornings is a backstop that lags behind: if it keeps rising, look at every
EC2 instance and EMR cluster again.

# Rubric summary

| Section | Points |
|---|---|
| Setup: roles, bucket, data, naming | 10 |
| Stage 1: predict, measure, explain | 20 |
| Stages 2a and 2b: two node counts, four gaps, keep the cluster up or launch it | 40 |
| Question 4: synthesis | 25 |
| Mechanics and screenshots | 5 |

Inside each stage, about a quarter of the marks go to the prediction, a quarter to the measurement,
and half to the explanation. The `rubric={...}` tag on each subsection gives the exact split. The prediction marks
buy a defended number, never a close one. A stage with no measurement cannot earn its explanation
marks, because there is no gap to explain.
